storeCredit.title: Store Credit Management System
storeCredit.description: A production app that replaced a paper credit ledger with a real-time system the whole store staff relies on daily.
storeCredit.overview: My family runs a small neighborhood grocery store that, like many in Costa Rica, extends informal credit to regular customers, known locally as "fiado". For years that credit was tracked in a paper notebook: illegible handwriting, lost pages, no way to audit who wrote what or when, and no backup if the notebook itself got damaged.
storeCredit.problem: The notebook worked until it didn't. Balances got miscounted, entries got disputed, and there was no way for more than one person to update it at the same time without creating conflicting records. I built this app to solve that specific problem, not to build a generic point-of-sale system.
storeCredit.role: I designed, built and deployed the entire system alone: data model, front end, notification service and infrastructure, based on how the store staff actually work day to day.
storeCredit.architectureIntro: A React client talks to Firebase directly for reads and writes. A separate Node.js service, running continuously with PM2 on a machine at the store, listens for database changes and triggers outbound notifications.
features: Real-time sync: multiple staff members can log sales and payments at the same time and see updates instantly on every device.
A single shared Firebase Authentication account with a PIN-based profile selector, so every action stays tied to a specific person without individual logins.
Full audit trail: nothing is permanently deleted, every record keeps who created or edited it and when, and suspended accounts can be restored.
Daily summary broken down by payment method, with 80mm thermal receipt printing and one-tap copy for WhatsApp.
Automatic WhatsApp and email alerts sent to each customer on every transaction, handled by the separate notification service so the client app never blocks on it.
Automatic daily database backup to Google Cloud Storage.
storeCredit.screenshotsIntro: The real usage flow, with customer names, phone numbers and profile photos blurred. Amounts without an attached name aren't sensitive.

gallery.profileSelector: Profile selector: whoever is on shift picks their name and enters their PIN.
gallery.clientList: Customer list sorted by debt, with the store's total outstanding credit.
gallery.clientDetail: A customer's detail view: current debt, credit limit, history, and the buttons to log a purchase or payment.
gallery.dailySummary: Daily summary by payment method, used to balance the register at closing.
gallery.dailyMovements: Feed of every transaction for the day, in chronological order.

storeCredit.outcome: The app has fully replaced the paper ledger and is used every day by store staff, with zero infrastructure cost since it runs entirely on free-tier services.
storeCredit.stack: React, Vite, Firebase (Realtime Database, Authentication), Node.js, PM2, Vercel with continuous deployment from GitHub, Google Cloud Storage for backups.

alwaysBarca.title: Always Barça
alwaysBarca.description: 33 seasons, five variables, one question: does transfer spending predict FC Barcelona's success better than academy usage, squad value, coaching, or the presidency?
alwaysBarca.question: What actually explains FC Barcelona's successful seasons: how much the club spends, or who is making the decisions? Net transfer spending, coaching continuity, academy usage, squad market value, and the presidency, tested against 33 seasons of sporting performance.
alwaysBarca.scope: 33 LaLiga seasons, 1993/94 through 2025/26. The analysis deliberately avoids isolating a single era (like only the Guardiola years): that would shrink the sample and weaken any statistical pattern. Coach and president are treated as variables across the full range instead, so both the general pattern and era-by-era comparisons stay visible.
dataSources: Performance and spending, 2014/15–2025/26 — automated, via football-data.co.uk and a Transfermarkt dataset on Kaggle
Spending and league-wide totals, 1993/94–2013/14 — manual collection from Transfermarkt, cross-validated against two separate views of the site with an exact match
Coaches and presidents — hand-built tables from public sources, including several mid-season changes verified by date
Academy players — 103 players from Wikipedia's "players formed at La Masía" table, cross-referenced against Transfermarkt appearances (reliable from 2012/13)
Squad market value — Transfermarkt, reliable coverage from 2012/13 onward
alwaysBarca.methodology: Performance is measured two ways: a continuous scale (points earned over the maximum possible that season, normalized so it's comparable across eras with different point systems and calendars) and a categorical one adjusted to a club of Barça's scale, where missing the Champions League already counts as a failed season. Comparing net spending across three decades is misleading on its own, since the transfer market has inflated much faster than the general economy, so spending is expressed as Barça's share of that season's total LaLiga transfer spending, the same principle the CIES Football Observatory uses to measure transfer market inflation. The same logic applies to squad market value. Pearson correlation measures the continuous variables (spending, academy use, squad value); coach and president are categorical, so a one-way ANOVA and its derived eta-squared (η²) put them on the same explained-variance scale as r², the detail that makes the final five-variable comparison honest instead of apples-to-oranges.
phase1Findings: Spending does not predict performance in a statistically significant way (r = 0.227, p = 0.204).
The coach is associated with more variation in performance than spending. Guardiola leads average performance (0.818, 3 titles in 4 seasons).
Attack explains more variance than defense (goals for r = 0.787 vs. goals against r = -0.660, both p < 0.001).
Three seasons carry explicitly documented atypical context: 2020/21 (pandemic, no fans at any match) and 2023/24–2024/25 (playing home matches at Montjuïc during the Camp Nou renovation).

Spending tends to concentrate at the start of a coaching cycle, more a renewal investment than a same-season predictor. Title seasons were won both with near-zero net spending (1997/98, 2025/26) and with significant investment.
phase2Findings: Academy usage doesn't predict performance either (r = 0.274, p = 0.344).
No simple link to titles: Koeman had the group's second-highest academy usage without winning a title in his 2 seasons; Flick combined the highest usage with the best title record (2 of 2).

2024/25 and 2025/26 closed with net transfer spending near zero and the two highest squad values in the range, driven by home-grown players with no transfer cost (Yamal, Gavi, Fermín López, Balde) and low-cost reacquisitions (Eric García, a free agent in 2021).
phase3Findings: Unlike spending and academy usage, squad market value shows a strong, significant correlation with performance (r = 0.753, p = 0.002), the strongest relationship found up to that phase.
Squad value measures an accumulated asset (a "stock" variable), while net spending measures a single summer's movement (a "flow" variable); the accumulated one predicts better.
phase4Findings: Important methodological correction: average spending per president isn't the same as good or bad management. Joan Laporta took office twice amid financial crises inherited from his predecessors (€180M spent by Gaspart in 2000-01; a €1.35B debt inherited from Bartomeu in 2021 that blocked Messi's renewal).

Gaspart and Laporta have almost the same average spending (7.5%) with opposite performance outcomes, evidence that average spending without context can lead to the wrong conclusion about a president's management.
Sandro Rosell leads average performance, spending, and squad value, inheriting an already solid base built during Laporta's first term.
alwaysBarca.summaryTitle: Consolidated summary: all five variables in the same unit
alwaysBarca.summaryIntro: To compare numeric variables (spending, academy, squad value) fairly against categorical ones (coach, president), every variable is expressed as variance explained: r² for the continuous ones, η² for the categorical ones, the same conceptual quantity.
alwaysBarca.conclusion: The coach is the variable that explains the most performance in the entire project, ahead even of accumulated squad value. The president comes in a close second. Spending and academy usage, the two "how much is invested" variables, land well below the other three, all of which relate to who decides or what talent is already in hand. Neither spending nor academy usage predicts Barça's performance well across 33 years of history. Accumulated squad value does, and who is in charge, coach first and president second, explains even more. Confirming this with causal rigor would require comparable data from other clubs, outside this project's scope.
alwaysBarca.limitations: Not every variable covers the same 33 seasons: performance, spending, coach and president are complete for 1993/94–2025/26, but academy usage and squad value only cover 2012/13–2025/26 (14 of 33 seasons), because Transfermarkt's appearance and valuation data isn't reliably covered before that. The gap was documented, not papered over with a lower-quality proxy. "Academy player" also has no single accepted definition, this project uses a broad one (anyone in Wikipedia's La Masía-formed table, including players who passed through the reserve team); a stricter definition would move the academy-usage numbers. One raw-data correction was applied by hand: the simplified standings model gave Barça a technical tie with Real Madrid in 2006/07, when the real title went to Madrid on head-to-head tiebreakers; the record was corrected to match reality. And throughout: correlation isn't causation, particularly for the presidency findings, where inherited financial context matters as much as the numbers themselves.
alwaysBarca.stack: Python and Pandas for data collection and cleaning, SciPy for the statistical tests (Pearson, ANOVA), Tableau Public for the four published dashboards.
alwaysBarca.dashboardsIntro: Four linked dashboards on Tableau Public, each covering a different phase of the analysis.

alwaysBarca.personalNote: This project didn't start from a convenient generic dataset, it started from being a culé. I'm writing this from Alajuela, Costa Rica, almost 8,970 km from Barcelona in a straight line, and that distance is part of the point: outside Spain, being a Barça fan loses the regional and political weight it carries at home, and what's left is something else entirely. It's a fitting moment to close this analysis too, with a new La Masía generation (Yamal, Cubarsí, Fermín López) already showing up in this project's own data.

messiOutlier.title: Messi: Outlier
messiOutlier.description: How singular is Messi's World Cup profile? Measured against the full population of 5,636 historical World Cup outfield players, not a handful of hand-picked comparisons.
messiOutlier.question: Does any historical World Cup player come close to combining, at the same time, the metrics that separate elite finishers, dribblers, chance creators and play organizers, or does Messi's profile stand out for appearing among the elite of several distinct functional roles at once?
messiOutlier.thesisTitle: A framing note, and the precise claim
messiOutlier.thesis: "Outlier" can suggest absolute uniqueness, and that's not quite what the data shows. Messi shares the highest ceiling actually observed in the population, elite status in 3 of 4 roles, with 7 other players. What the data does show, and what holds up under every threshold and sample-size cut tested, is more precise: across the full 1966–2026 World Cup population, no player's profile clearly exceeds or consistently matches his on the measure that matters most, average role percentile among players with a real career-length sample. That's a claim about the absence of a better-supported rival, not about mathematical uniqueness.
approach: Players are compared by functional role (finisher, dribbler, chance creator, play organizer), not nominal position, since a player's position often doesn't match what they actually do on the pitch. 16 metrics, checked against the data provider's own glossary, are assigned across the four roles.

Metrics are normalized per 90 minutes, aggregated at player-career level (one row per player, summing every World Cup match from 1966 to 2026), with a 270-minute minimum (three full matches) chosen by testing where small-sample noise actually stabilizes. Higher floors (900, 1500 minutes) are used throughout as a transparency check, not a replacement.
"Elite" is defined by percentile, not a fixed top-N, tested at the 90th, 95th and 99th percentiles rather than committing to one cutoff.
Percentiles are calculated against the full relevant player population (5,636 outfield players; 2,488 meet the 270-minute threshold), not only against a few reference players.
The hypothesis was allowed to fail, and did, in its strongest form: no player, including Messi, reaches elite status in all four roles at once at a genuine elite threshold.
messiOutlier.rolesIntro: Functional roles, not fixed pitch positions, since the same player shifts position across a career.

roles.finisher: Finisher — converts chances into goals: goals, xG, shot conversion, shots on target.
roles.unbalancer: Dribbler — creates individual danger by taking on defenders: successful dribbles, fouls drawn, progressive carries.
roles.playmaker: Chance creator — creates the direct chance: assists, key passes, xA, big chances created.
roles.orchestrator: Play organizer — circulates the ball and progresses the attack from deeper zones: progressive passes, completion rate, passes into the final third.

messiOutlier.extraction: Confirmed, against a 1986 Maradona match and the 2022 final, that SofaScore's internal API has comparable event-level detail across the entire 1966–2026 range. Full extraction: 900 matches, 5,636 outfield players at career level.
messiOutlier.correlation: The three attacking roles (finisher, dribbler, chance creator) correlate moderately with each other (0.49–0.58). Play organizer is nearly independent of all three (0.02–0.30), confirming it as a genuinely distinct skill dimension — which led to a prediction, made before running any numbers, that organizer would be Messi's relative weak point.
messiOutlier.centralFinding: No player in the population reaches elite status in all 4 roles at a genuine threshold (90th percentile or higher). The real ceiling, elite in 3 of 4 roles, is shared by 8 players; Messi is one of them, with by far the largest career sample (6 World Cups, 34 matches, 3,054 minutes). Among players with a real career-length sample (900+ minutes), Messi has the highest average role percentile in the entire population. Maradona is a genuine, non-cherry-picked runner-up, with the gap explained almost entirely by play organizer, exactly as predicted in Phase 4. Cristiano Ronaldo, with a nearly identical career sample to Messi's, has the lowest average role score in the project's comparison sets, direct evidence the finding isn't simply a function of playing many World Cups.
messiOutlier.specialists: Building the reference set for the radar charts surfaced its own finding: the organizer-role leader at the base 270-minute threshold turned out to be driven by a single match of high-volume, low-threat passing (Spain's 2018 round-of-16 exit to Russia), not genuine organizing quality. A stricter 900-minute floor was applied specifically for choosing which players get shown as "leaders."
messiOutlier.conclusion: No player's profile in the 1966–2026 World Cup population clearly exceeds or consistently matches Messi's across the four functional roles measured here. This isn't a claim of mathematical uniqueness, several other players share the observed ceiling, and Maradona is a real, well-supported runner-up. It's a claim about the absence of a better-supported rival, on the most robust measure this project could construct: average role percentile among players with a genuine career-length sample, tested across multiple percentile thresholds and multiple minimum-minutes floors, none of which changed the result. The one relative weakness found, play organizer, was predicted before the data was ever run, which strengthens the finding rather than undermining it. The declared limitation stands: this measures roughly 6 months of accumulated football (Messi's six World Cups) against a much longer career, a deliberate scope choice, not an oversight.
messiOutlier.closingTitle: Closing a chapter, while this project was closing too
messiOutlier.closing: On August 31, 2026, while this project was in the middle of being built, Lionel Messi officially announced his retirement from the Argentina national team, after playing his sixth World Cup. At 39 years old, in what turned out to be his last tournament, he scored 8 goals and gave 4 assists in 8 matches, taking Argentina all the way to the final. Those are numbers most footballers in history never reach even at their physical peak, and he produced them at the end of his career. His World Cup story is closed for good: six tournaments between 2006 and 2026, 34 matches, 21 goals. This wasn't planned. The project started as a Data Analytics portfolio exercise, and it ended up coinciding, without anyone intending it, with the real and final close of the World Cup career it analyzes. From here on, Messi's World Cup numbers won't change again, so this is a finished, complete record, not a snapshot of something still in motion. Thank you, Leo. And I will always carry December 18, 2022 in my heart, the day you fulfilled your childhood dream.
dataSources: SofaScore — the project's sole data source. Match-level stats (passes, duels, touches, dribbles, shots) accessed through its internal API (no official public API exists), using the ScraperFC library, validated first against a 1986 Maradona match and the 2022 final.
FBref and Kaggle were considered as complementary sources early on but weren't ultimately needed; SofaScore's historical coverage covered everything the project's metrics required.
